target_customer: Web developers needing client-side JavaScript error monitoring
problem: Client-side JavaScript errors in production are hard to see; developers had to wrap code in handlers by hand.
business_model: SaaS proxy with free tier (under 1,000 page views a month) and paid tiers from $30 a month for 10,000 page views (TechCrunch 2011-08)
product_category: JavaScript error monitoring and debugging proxy

technical_complexity.rationale: A proxy that rewrites JavaScript to inject error reporting, minify and cache it, and compile CoffeeScript, with failover to the origin server (TechCrunch 2011-08).

defensibility.rationale: Instrumentation snippets are easy to copy; nothing in the sources suggests a data or integration moat.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No acquisition of Proxino found; an aggregator says the market got crowded with competitors such as Sentry before the company ended (weak source).

market_need_then: TechCrunch (2011-08-22) says the founders saw few good tools for detecting browser errors, with developers relying on manual handlers or cross-browser test suites; demand was asserted by the founders, not measured.

brand_strength.rationale: No source on brand strength found; not rated.

outcome_analysis: The cause of Proxino's shutdown is not public: the YC directory lists it as Inactive, the site returned 503, and no post-mortem or acquisition was found. A startup-failure aggregator gives a 2014 end and about $120K burned and says the market became crowded (unsourced), so no failure factors are asserted. The proxy approach had little moat against error-tracking services.
notes: Directory status Inactive; exit.type=shutdown inferred from that status, date and reason not public (an aggregator says 2014, unverified, so exit.date left null).
